name: Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders): advocacy and research
beneficiaries_note: Our build: MSF Access's TB price cuts (77% of the result) spread over the high-burden countries that buy the tests and drugs (India, Indonesia, the Philippines, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, South Africa, the DRC; our weights by TB burden); awareness-raising (17%) over the crisis countries of MSF's medical model, equally; DNDi (6%) over the DRC, Sudan and Kenya (sleeping sickness and leishmaniasis). A judgment.
summary: Besides medical care, Médecins Sans Frontières spends about 65 million euros a year on awareness-raising (public communications and witnessing), MSF Access (advocacy for affordable medicines and tests) and a grant to the Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative. None publishes outcome data, so each is built from the research on its kind of work and counted at half by the shared missing-data slider: MSF Access as the buyers' savings from the TB price cuts it campaigned for in 2019-2025 (Xpert tests, bedaquiline), awareness-raising as the extra humanitarian funding its share of news coverage brings, DNDi at a drug-development partnership's measured return. The result is far below the site's health median (under a tenth): advocacy's effects are spread over many actors and MSF's share of them is small, the evidence is thin (all three branches discounted for missing data), and past wins count at the shared share of the average a next dollar does. The result is mostly uncertainty; the biggest questions are how much of the price cuts advocacy caused and MSF's share of it, and how far news coverage moves aid.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: Three branches. MSF Access (the template's policy rows): the price cuts won in 2019-2025, valued as buyers' savings. Awareness-raising: the extra humanitarian funding its communications bring, from the research on media and aid. DNDi: MSF's grant at a drug-development partnership's measured return, in DALYs.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch has its own evidence, counterfactual, attribution and missing-data rows; the canonical rows are their outcome-weighted averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. rows.explainer: About 20 million cartridges procured in 2022 (the Global Fund's announcement of the cut, which expects 'more than 5 million more tests' from the savings, about $40 million a year at $7.97). rows.label: Bedaquiline price cut of August 2023: savings (US$)

source.title: CIDRAP, Major price cut announced for critical drug for resistant TB (2023)
source.quote: the $8 million in savings generated by the bedaquiline price cut

rows.explainer: The Global Drug Facility's tender cut Johnson & Johnson's bedaquiline from $289 to $130 a six-month course (55%), a month after the primary patent expired; MSF had campaigned against J&J's secondary patents. GDF estimated $8 million in savings, enough for 51,000 more treatments; the source states no period, but $8 million over $159 a course is about 50,000 courses, a year of GDF's orders, so it is counted as a year's. Low end if it was for a longer period.

rows.label: Other price cuts in the period, relative to these two
rows.explainer: MSF Access and its partners pressed for more cuts in 2019-2025 that aren't counted above: the BPaLM regimen for drug-resistant TB (38% cheaper through GDF in 2024, towards the $500 regimen target MSF set), pneumococcal vaccine for humanitarian groups, and the lenacapavir and HIV-test campaigns. Our judgment, half as much again; 0 if only the two counted wins count, 1.5 if the others were as big together.

rows.label: MSF Access: share of the savings that fall to the Global Fund and other donors' budgets
rows.explainer: The Global Fund pays for most Xpert cartridges and GDF purchases of TB drugs in low-income countries; governments pay the rest, more in middle-income countries such as India and South Africa. Our judgment, 65%.

rows.label: Share of the 2025 appeals' requirements met

source.title: ALNAP, The State of the Humanitarian System 2026, 1.2 Who has been prioritised?
source.quote: Only 35% of funding requirements within OCHA managed Humanitarian Response Plans

rows.explainer: From OCHA's Financial Tracking Service, partial-year data for 2025.

rows.label: Share of that funding going to crises MSF works in and speaks about
rows.explainer: MSF's largest programmes (the DRC, Sudan, Palestine, South Sudan, Nigeria, Yemen, Chad, the Central African Republic, Afghanistan, Niger) are among the largest appeals; Ukraine and Syria too. Our judgment, 70%.

rows.label: Awareness: rise in a crisis's funding per rise in its news coverage (elasticity)
rows.explainer: Rost & Clarke (2025, https://doi.org/10.1111/dpr.12819), on the share of humanitarian appeals funded: 'Increasing the number of news articles about the humanitarian situation in a country from 100 per year to 1,000 would be associated with an appeal that is 6 percentage points better funded' (24 points from 100 to 100,000). The steps are 6, 8 and 10 points per tenfold rise (100 to 1,000, 1,000 to 10,000, 10,000 to 100,000 articles), so the slope grows with coverage: 2.6 to 4.3 points per log unit, an elasticity of 0.07 to 0.12 at the 35% of requirements met in 2025. MSF's crises are among the most covered, the middle step's 3.5 points (0.10) the best fit. The high end from studies of disaster news: one more minute of nightly news raised tsunami donations by about 2.5% (Brown & Minty 2008, https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2325-8012.2008.tb00889.x) and US relief depends on whether other news crowds a disaster out (Eisensee & Strömberg 2007, https://doi.org/10.1162/qjec.122.2.693). Donor officials say only emergency top-ups respond, not annual allocations (Scott et al. 2021, https://doi.org/10.1080/1461670x.2021.2013129). Best 0.1.

source.title: Rost & Clarke 2025, Why do governments fund some humanitarian appeals but not others? (Development Policy Review 43, e12819)
source.quote: Increasing the number of news articles about the humanitarian situation in a country from 100 per year to 1,000 would be associated with an appeal that is 6 percentage points better funded.

rows.label: Awareness: share of these crises' international coverage MSF's communications add
rows.explainer: MSF is among the most quoted humanitarian sources, but coverage follows events and journalists' own reporting. Our judgment, 1.5% more coverage than without MSF's communications; 5% for the crises it is nearly alone in (eastern Chad, the Central African Republic).

rows.label: Awareness: share of the extra funding that is new rather than taken from other crises
rows.explainer: Funding a crisis gains from coverage often comes from donors' reserves or from other crises (Scott et al. 2021, above); money moved between crises counts only for its gain, taken as none. Our judgment, 30%.

rows.label: Awareness: value of a humanitarian dollar as a multiple of cash to the very poor
rows.explainer: Humanitarian aid is largely food, cash, health care and shelter for people in acute need, after agencies' overheads. Our judgment, about as good as cash given directly (1×), from half to twice.

rows.label: Awareness: value of a humanitarian dollar (units of value)
rows.explainer: The multiple × the site's value of a dollar given as cash (@cash.uov_per_dollar).

rows.label: Awareness: other goals reached, as a share of the funding effect
rows.explainer: Témoignage also presses parties to conflicts and governments: protests over attacks on hospitals (behind UN Security Council resolution 2286 of 2016), access for aid, policy on migrants. None has a measure; our judgment, half as much again as the funding effect, up to twice.

rows.label: Awareness: value of a year's communications (units of value, before adjustments)
rows.formula: aw_requirements_usd * aw_share_funded * aw_share_msf_crises * aw_media_elasticity * aw_coverage_share * aw_new_money_share * aw_value_per_dollar * (1 + aw_other_benefits_share)
rows.explainer: Funding to the crises × the funding's response to coverage × the coverage MSF adds × the new money's share × the value of a humanitarian dollar, plus the other goals. A year's flow against a year's spending.

rows.label: Healthy years averted by a product development partnership's drugs (MMV, 2000-2023)

source.title: Christen et al. 2026, Measuring the impact of global research and development investment in product development partnerships: return on investment in antimalarial drug development (Lancet Global Health)
source.quote: averted an estimated 1·6 million deaths and 87 million DALYs for a cost of delivery estimated at $785 million

rows.explainer: The one published measure of what a not-for-profit drug developer's products did: Medicines for Malaria Venture, DNDi's sister partnership (ASAQ, one of DNDi's treatments, is an antimalarial of the same kind). Range: the paper's low and high DALY scenarios (Table 4: benefit-cost ratios of 8.98 and 16.32 against 12.99, costs fixed).

rows.label: That partnership's R&D funding, 2000-2023 (US$)

source.title: Christen et al. 2026 (Lancet Global Health)
source.quote: Total investment received was US$2·3 billion over the study period

rows.explainer: MMV's total funding over the study period.

rows.label: Cost of delivering that partnership's drugs (US$)

source.title: Christen et al. 2026 (Lancet Global Health)
source.quote: for a cost of delivery estimated at $785 million

rows.explainer: Others' money behind the same DALYs: research gets its share of all the resources (Convention 2).

rows.label: Healthy years averted per dollar of the partnership's R&D, its share of the resources
rows.explainer: DALYs over all the money behind them (R&D and delivery), so the R&D dollar gets its share.

rows.label: DNDi's healthy years per dollar as a share of MMV's
rows.explainer: DNDi's 13 treatments since 2003 are mostly for diseases with far smaller burdens than malaria (sleeping sickness, leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, paediatric HIV), most of them improved uses of existing drugs; its antimalarial ASAQ reached hundreds of millions of patients but beside other artemisinin combinations. Our judgment, 15% of MMV's return per dollar.

rows.label: DNDi: years from R&D funding to health gains
rows.explainer: MMV's funding started in 2000 and its first products launched in 2009; DNDi's ASAQ came four years after its founding (2007), fexinidazole fifteen (2018). Our judgment, eight years.

rows.label: DNDi: discount for the wait
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate.

rows.label: DNDi: healthy years averted by MSF's grant (DALYs, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The grant × the partnership's past return per dollar, scaled to DNDi's portfolio, discounted for the wait until the treatments are used.

rows.label: MSF Access: trust in the savings and their value
rows.explainer: The prices and the 2022 volumes are published; the doubt is about the savings themselves: volumes actually ordered at the new price, other cartridges (MTB/XDR at $14.90) staying dear, and prices reviewed yearly. The value of a dollar saved is the site's shared figure, not doubted here. Our judgment, 0.9.

rows.label: MSF Access: share of the cuts that wouldn't have come yet without advocacy
rows.explainer: Each cut counts the shared years brought forward; this is the share of it that wouldn't have come yet without the campaigners. Bedaquiline's came with the primary patent's expiry, GDF's competitive tender and Lupin's generic ready at $194 (a lower share); Xpert's after four years of the coalition's pressure with no competitor, though the agreement was the Global Fund's, Stop TB's and USAID's with Danaher. Our judgment, half.

rows.label: MSF Access: MSF's share of the advocates' resources
rows.explainer: Time for $5 was coordinated by the MSF Access Campaign, Partners in Health and Treatment Action Group with more than 150 civil society organisations; the Xpert agreement was the Global Fund's, Stop TB's and USAID's with Danaher, and the bedaquiline price was negotiated by the Global Drug Facility with USAID and the Global Fund, with activists' patent challenges in India and South Africa. Our judgment, a quarter.

rows.label: Missing data: MSF Access
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12): the savings are published, but the share caused by advocacy and MSF's part in it are judgments, and no study measures what campaigns do to prices, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: MSF Access: adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Awareness: trust in the media-funding evidence for MSF's communications
rows.explainer: The studies are of disaster news and private donations or US relief, not of an aid agency's communications on conflicts. Our judgment, 0.6.

rows.label: Awareness: share of the coverage others wouldn't have produced
rows.explainer: 1: the coverage share above is already what MSF's communications add over what other agencies and journalists would have produced (Convention 5), so it isn't asked again here.

rows.label: Awareness: MSF's share of the resources behind the extra coverage
rows.explainer: The coverage is journalists' and editors' work too. Our judgment, three quarters.

rows.label: Missing data: awareness-raising
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12): MSF publishes no outcome data for its communications; the whole chain is our judgment on the literature on media and aid, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: Awareness: adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: DNDi: trust in the partnership's measured return
rows.explainer: Christen et al.'s DALYs are modelled from drug volumes and efficacy by authors close to the partnership. Our judgment, 0.7.

rows.label: DNDi: share of its treatments' gains other developers wouldn't have brought
rows.explainer: Christen et al.'s DALYs are already gains over the most likely older treatment (artemether-lumefantrine tablets, intravenous quinine), but they credit the partnership with all of them; others might have developed some of the drugs. Our judgment, half.

rows.label: Money moved or raised for other charities (US$)
rows.explainer: MSF raises money for its own work and grants little to others (DNDi's grant is a branch above), so none is valued as money moved.

rows.label: Money moved per dollar of the charity's cost
rows.explainer: Context, and the donors' share of the resources with credit by share of resources on.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium's seasonal malaria chemoprevention, Helen Keller Intl's vitamin A, New Incentives), each at its result on this site under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: This organisation moves money only to global health and poverty charities, so a dollar moved is valued at that destination alone (GiveWell's Top Charities, live).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
